question: None shared. P-95 ranks expert-selected neuropsychological feature groups against neuroradiological groups (DTI, visual rating scales, subcortical volumes) for 3-class AD / MCI / control diagnosis in a Novi Sad memory-clinic cohort of 90. P-96 screens for an MMSE-defined 'high-risk MCI' label from seven routine physical-examination and blood variables in Chinese community cohorts (CHARLS, Yiwu). The task (3-class diagnosis vs binary screening), label and channels (NP + MRI vs blood/anthropometry) all differ.
metric: Mismatch. The record's claimed quantity is a modality ranking (NP vs MRI) in each paper, but P-96 contains no such ranking: it has no MRI and no neuropsychological predictor. P-95's metrics are 3-class accuracy and weighted AUROC; P-96's are binary AUROC and accuracy.

figures.P-95: NP better than NR within the cohort: best NP combination 71.11-79.78% accuracy across seven classifiers (Table 7); most NR groups below 50% accuracy (text; NR left out of Table 7); all 482 features 66.22-81.00% accuracy.
figures.P-96: Random forest for MMSE-defined high-risk MCI: training AUROC 0.93 (0.91-0.95), accuracy 85.5%; external AUROC 0.83 and 0.87. No MRI-vs-NP comparison exists.

matched_figure_check: Not applicable: one side of the claimed comparison (an MRI-vs-NP ranking in P-96) does not exist, so there is no figure to match.
performance_validity: Not a like-for-like performance comparison. In any case neither paper reaches 0.97: P-95's best AUROC is 94.95%; P-96's is AUROC 0.93, with external validation.
reason: P-96 uses no MRI and no neuropsychological predictor; the MMSE only defines its outcome. So the recorded 'MRI outperforms NP (79% vs 72%)' has no counterpart, and there is no second result to set against P-95. The papers also answer different questions: 3-class clinical diagnosis in a Serbian clinic, against community screening for a psychometric label from blood and physical-examination data.
